value.overview: The Rufous Motmot (Baryphthengus martii) is a large forest-dwelling member of the motmot family, recognized by its warm cinnamon-rufous plumage, black facial mask, green wings, blue-green lower belly, and long dark tail. It is associated with humid lowland and foothill forests from Central America to western and Amazonian South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of the Caribbean lowlands and adjacent foothills, where it is most often found in mature, shaded forest and advanced secondary growth.
value.classification: The Rufous Motmot belongs to the family Momotidae in the order Coraciiformes. It is one of two recognized species in the genus Baryphthengus; the other is the Rufous-capped Motmot of southeastern South America.
value.identification: This is one of the largest motmots in its range, with a very long, graduated tail. Adults have a cinnamon-rufous head and underparts, a broad black mask, a small black central breast spot, green wings and flanks, a greenish-blue lower belly, and dark blue tail and flight feathers. The bill and legs are black. Costa Rican birds may show racket-like bare tail tips, although this feature can vary geographically; young birds are duller and usually lack the breast spot and tail rackets.
value.rangeHabitat: The Rufous Motmot ranges from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, then south through Colombia and western Ecuador into parts of the Amazon Basin. In Costa Rica it is a resident species concentrated on the Caribbean slope, including humid lowlands and foothills, generally from near sea level to about 900 meters in the north and locally higher, approaching 1,400 meters toward southern areas near Panama. It uses tall wet forest, mature shaded secondary growth, forest edges, and partly cleared habitats such as shaded plantations.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not known to undertake regular long-distance migration. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from March through June. The nest is a long, often winding burrow excavated in a stream-bank ravine, earthen bank, or suitable cavity. Burrows may extend several meters, and both parents participate in feeding the young. The eggs are poorly documented, so details such as clutch size and incubation period should be treated as incompletely known. Pairs typically remain near forested banks or other protected nesting sites during reproduction.
value.dietFeeding: The Rufous Motmot eats a varied diet of large insects, including beetles, along with other arthropods, small vertebrates, and fruits. It usually waits quietly on a shaded perch before making short flights to capture prey from foliage, branches, or the ground. It may forage in the understory and sometimes follows army ants, taking prey disturbed by the advancing ants. In Costa Rica it can also hunt in adjoining shaded plantations and other forest-associated habitats.
value.behavior: Rufous Motmots are generally solitary or occur in pairs. They often sit motionless in shaded vegetation, scanning the understory, and may be difficult to detect until they call or fly. Their vocalizations are low, repeated hoots or hollow notes. The species commonly forages from perches and may descend into dense understory or to the ground. Like other motmots, it may wag its long tail, although this display is less conspicuous when the bird is hidden in forest shade.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
